newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand's Advance Agro sees turnaround in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Thailand's Advance Agro sees turnaround in 1997.

text.p: Thailand's leading but loss-making pulp and paper producer Advance Agro Plc hopes to turn up profits later this year on the back of improving world pulp and paper prices and by market expansion.
Yotin Dumnerncharnvanit, the firm's managing director, said the company aimed to beat a slowdown in paper demand in Thailand by boosting exports to regional and European markets.

The company expected to export at least 200,000 tonnes of paper this year and earn around 4.0 billion baht ($160 million) in foreign currency compared with paltry exports of only 21,000 tonnes last year.

"We believe pulp and paper prices have bottomed out and are recovering. Prices have increased by 10 percent this year which should benefit us. We hope to be able to turn loss into profit by Q3 or Q4," Yotin told Reuters in an interview.
Advance Agro's pulp and paper mills at this southeastern province have a combined capacity to produce 470,000 tonnes of printing and writing paper annually.

The firm produces its own short-fibre pulp from trees harvested in its Eucalyptus plantation. It also buys from farmers, most of whom plant cloned seedlings purchased from the company on a commitment to sell to it on a long-term basis.

The company's second pulp mill with capacity of 255,000 tonnes per year is scheduled to be completed by end-1997. Advance Agro is also planning to jointly invest with the Chinese government to set up a 27 billion baht, 700,000 tonne-a-year pulp plant in Thailand.
In 1996, the company posted losses of 913 million baht. The 1997 first quarter loss widened to 317.4 million baht from 151.9 million baht during the same period last year.
Yotin blamed the losses on high start-up costs, bearish paper prices and foreign exchange losses. The company started running at full capacity and exporting only in 1996.

Pulp prices -- a key indicator for the volatile paper industry business cycle -- plunged in late 1995 and last year. They started picking up in March with long-fibre pulp now being traded around $580 per tonne from $520 earlier this year.
The company's biggest markets are in Asia, especially China, which has recorded strong demand growth for paper over the past decade. Asia accounted for 50 percent of Advance's exports.
The firm's export prices were around $800 per tonne on an FOB basis this year compared with $700 last year.
However, the company in April started expanding the market to European countries such as Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and Belgium in April.

"This is a very good sign and it gives us an advantage over a major competitor like Indonesia. Europeans are very particular about environment and their purchases indicate they trust that our products are environmentally friendly," Yotin said.
"In May alone we exported around 80 percent of our capacity," he added.

But analysts cautioned that although Advance Agro has solid cost management due to its relatively modern production technology, it was, like every paper producer, extremely susceptible to the cyclical nature of the industry.
"The company's earnings are tied mostly to the world paper prices. The problem is we don't know if the cycle has really bottomed out," said a National Finance and Securities analyst.

Moreover, the company was likely to face tougher competition from other low-cost producers in the region in the near future as paper was one of the products on the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA)'s fast-track list for tariff reduction within the grouping, analysts said.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations comprises Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Indonesia and Singapore. Burma, Laos and Cambodia will join in July.
